newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street Journal honored for its AIDS reporting.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street Journal honored for its AIDS reporting.

text.p: It was the year of the presidential election and the year when scientists found an expensive and complicated way to stop the virus that causes AIDS from spreading out of control.
For the Pulitzer Prize board the national reporting story of 1996 was AIDS and Monday it gave a ground-breaking Wall Street Journal series its award for National Reporting.

Runners-up in the category were Ronald Brownstein of the Los Angeles Times for his presidential campaign coverage and Bill Moushey of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette for a series on the failures of the witness protection programme.

The Journal was cited for 10 stories, including five by Michael Waldholz, its science writer, and one by David Sanford, for his story about living with the HIV infection and gaining a renewed life thanks to the expensive cocktail of drugs that have to be taken at odd hours of the day.
"I went from feeling I was dying to feeling I was healthy and no longer dwelling on dying," he said in an interview.
Sanford wrote about his experiences taking 17 different pills three times a day in a page one story headlined: "Back to the Future: One Man's Aids Tale Shows How Quickly Epidemic is Turned."
Waldholz said the discovery that the cockktail of drugs was working was a bittersweet victory because the drugs are expensive and many people will not be able to afford them.
